cultivar: Zhenghe Dabai ('da cha', the big-leaf tippy component) blended with local small-leaf cai cha ('xiao cha') for aroma
processing: Fully oxidised gongfu black: the thick Zhenghe Dabai leaf is withered, rolled firmly, oxidised and dried, then traditionally blended with a smaller-leaf, more aromatic batch and sorted.
harvest_season: Spring, late April into May; Zhenghe sits high, so picking is later than in coastal Fujian and summer lots are coarser.
appearance_dry: Thick, fat, tightly twisted strands, black with plentiful golden tips.
appearance_liquor: Deep red and bright, the darkest of the three Fujian gongfu teas.
appearance_wet: Large, thick, copper-red leaves with plump buds.
taste_profile: Full and malty with caramel and sweet potato, a rose- or violet-like floral note from the small-leaf component, and a firm, sweet finish.

brewing.notes: Handles water near the boil better than its two siblings. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes; the fullest-bodied of the three and the one that takes milk.

vintage_note: Sold by the current year's spring harvest and graded by tip content; the sturdy leaf keeps well for two years in a sealed bag, but it is not aged and there is no vintage market.
description:
Zhenghe Gongfu is the big-boned member of the Fujian gongfu trio, from Zhenghe County in the hills of northern Fujian, next door to Wuyi. It has been made since the 1870s, a generation after Tanyang and Bailin, and it was built on a different plant: Zhenghe Dabai, a large-leaf, thick-budded cultivar that gives weight and golden tips, which makers traditionally blend with a little small-leaf local tea for fragrance.

The process is standard gongfu black – withering, firm rolling, oxidation, drying, sorting – but the two components are often made separately and married at the end: 'da cha' from Dabai for body and tips, 'xiao cha' from the population bushes for aroma. The result is a tea with more tannin and colour than Bailin, more weight than Tanyang, and a floral note that sits over malt rather than honey.

Expect caramel, sweet potato and malt up front, a rose- or violet-like floral in the middle steeps and a firm, sweet finish that lasts; it runs seven steeps with water near the boil and makes the best milk-tea pot of the three. The mistake is to brew it as delicately as a bud tea: it wants heat.

It is sold by the current spring harvest, graded by tips, and because Zhenghe is also a white-tea county (Zhenghe white is the Dabai cultivar's other life), many makers sell both. Look for thick, glossy, well-twisted leaf with real golden tips; thin, flat leaf means summer material or a different county. Zhenghe gongfu is less famous than Tanyang and therefore usually better value for the same quality.

If you drink Assam or Ceylon and want a Chinese black with similar weight but less bite, this is the one to try first.
sources_note: Origin is usually given as 1874 or 'Guangxu era'; stated as 1870s. The da cha / xiao cha blending practice is traditional and not every modern maker follows it.
